I always liked the argument that my philosophy professor used, this is a simplistic argument.

  1. Define God as perfect.
  2. Realize something that exists is more perfect in that it has existence over something that does not.
  3. Conclude that since God is perfect, he/she must exist.

Which leads to the counterarguments:

  1. There's nothing which establishes that the definition is well-formed, ie if the followup arguments establish that God exists even when God cannot exist, then that just means that God is not well-defined.
  2. To say that existing is more perfect than not existing is a subjective claim rather than solid logic. If the existence of God implies the existence of eternal suffering, for example, then it's not as clear that existence is more perfect than non-existence.
  3. Accepting the conclusion doesn't imply anything about the nature of God. For example, you may have just proven that "nothingness" exists, and given it the name "God."

There is no solid proof either way and you know it.

Logic and faith are diametrically opposite concepts; logic derives truth from evidence, fact and reason, whereas faith by definition is believing something in the absence of all those things. To believers, your query doesn't make sense. To give you an example, think about this question: Why should anyone be moral?

It seems silly at first glance; one should moral because it's the right thing to do. But that's not really satisfying. All we've managed to do is say that a=a, without explaining why it is a categorical imperative. What makes something right? Ethicists have developed lots of theories, but all of those with traction have one thing in common: they rely on logic. The reason a given action is moral is because it is logical. When someone asks "why should I be moral", they are really asking, "why should I be logical"? The very question undermines the apparatus of reason that supports any arguments for being logical, and therefor is entirely nonsensical. You should be logical because its logical to do so.

Returning to the question of faith, you might ask a believer, "Why should I have believe?" For them, the answer is simple: because in order to have faith, you must have faith. Perhaps Voltaire put it best when he said, "Faith consists in believing when it is beyond the power of reason to believe."

Having faith is just making an assumption. That is, you collect evidence of various sorts, qualities, and quantities. You compare the evidence in support of a belief with the evidence for non-belief or belief in an alternative theory. At some point you make a decision to believe, to reject the belief, or to belief in an alternative theory.

This process is carried out everyday in every momement of our lives. We believe we wake up in our apartment. We believe its our car in the garage. We believe we are eating real food, etc. Yet we do not know that any of these things are true. Maybe our friends are playing a prank and carried you into another apartment over night. Maybe a similar looking car is sitting in your garage, but not specifically yours. Maybe we are in the matrix and your avatar is eating the food (which is virtual food to begin with).

The same is true of belief in a higher power. Each individual collects evidence then chooses to form a belief based on that evidence.

The gap between evidence and a belief is filled with assumptions. For a believer in evolution, you assume carbon dating is correct. You assume the science text you read about carbon dating was not written by a science hack who just wanted to publish a paper to get promoted. You assume the papers were peer reviewed. You assume the peer reviewers were properly qualified. You make hundreds of thousands of assumption in order to make the jump between evidence to a belief.

Again, assumptions are just the scientific word for having "faith"

Let me give you what I believe Descartes' reasoning was, because I think it is quite clever.

One of the main intellectual projects of the early humanist movement reached a climax in the logical-positivism of the early twentieth century. The idea was basically twofold: 1) Everything can be logically described, and 2) Only logical descriptions of things have meaning.

(Interestingly enough, as an aside, most people subscribe to the first, atheists still tend to subscribe to the second as well in the face of evidence, while Quine rejected the first but maintained the second, something which I have considerable sympathy for)

The problem is that, since Russell's paradox it increasingly became clear that logical positivism was bound to become an utter failure. Attempts were still made, and dismally failed, but it was not until Goedel's incompleteness theorem and Tarski's undefinability problem that it became clear that logical positivism (what many atheists still subscribe) is actually irrational.

In order to completely explain the universe you require something "out of system". This is actually baked into things like the multi-verse theory. There is no real distinction between that and religion from a scientific point of view, aside from the fact that the multi-verse is easier for many scientists to accept for aesthetic reasons.

This was presaged by Descartes three centuries earlier. His solution was just to say "God exists but would not lie". That means that we are free to accept the existence of "out of system" entities and still maintain the integrity of "within system" explanations. So yes, if a "god" exists it would be a "god of the gaps", but the kicker is that we can be more sure of the existence of the gaps than we can be about the nature of reality itself.

If believing in a "god" pleases you and does not harm others then you are absolutely every bit as entitled to doing so as a PhD'd physicist is entitled to believing in the multi-verse.
